detail.title: Human Time as an Economic Asset: How Innovation Creates Value and Why It Should Be Measured

keywords: human time as an economic asset
revealed preference and the value of time

detail.abstract: The stock of human time serves a dual role in the economy: it is the ultimate source of social welfare and a principal input into producing it. It is therefore central to economic progress. Raising its value, both at the intensive margin through gains in productivity and at the extensive margin through gains in longevity, could generate substantial increases in short-run and long-run welfare. Yet no one systematically tracks the value of human time, and this paper argues that economists should. The paper makes five contributions. First, it shows that human time is a personal, national, and global asset: a rough estimate places the value of the U.S. time stock at roughly $4.5 quadrillion, dwarfing conventional assets such as the housing stock, fixed capital, and the value of publicly traded companies. Second, it develops a framework in which human time is two-dimensional, combining chronological time with the brain activity, which includes the allocation of attention, that occurs over time. Third, it uses this framework to identify nine overlapping sources of disruptive innovation that raise the value of human time, pointing in several cases to rigorous economic studies that document the gains. Fourth, it shows that the existing economic toolkit, such as value-of-life studies, can deliver revealed-preference estimates of changes in the value of time at the intensive and extensive margins. Finally, it argues that it is worthwhile and feasible to construct a "time score card" that tracks changes in the value of human time using revealed preference, with money as a common numeraire. Such a measure would fill gaps left by conventional metrics such as GDP, which miss key aspects of human time; it would provide a rigorous proxy for long-run welfare; and it could guide economic policy, including investments in public goods that raise the value of human time. Economists, the paper concludes, would do well to devote more research to human time as a measurable improvable asset that is critical to well-being and incorporate human time more rigorously into existing fields such as macroeconomics.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Inventory Control in Three-Echelon Supply Chains with Bypass Routing

detail.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Inventory Control in Three-Echelon Supply Chains with Bypass Routing
detail.abstract: We study a finite-horizon, periodic-review, capacitated three-echelon supply chain inventory problem with multiple factories, distribution centers, and local warehouses, in which replenishment can follow either standard hierarchical routes or direct factory-to-warehouse bypass routes. The resulting decision problem jointly integrates production planning, shipment allocation, inventory control, and routing under stochastic and seasonal demand, deterministic or stochastic lead-time regimes, and networkwide inventory interactions. To address this problem, we formulate it as a stochastic control problem in which routing decisions are represented by binary variables, and we develop a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach based on proximal policy optimization (PPO). We compare alternative observation and action parameterizations, including full versus reduced state representations and purely continuous versus mixed action designs. We then benchmark the learned policies against an expected-value problem baseline and optimized static inventory policies, such as (s,Q) and basestock rules. Numerical experiments on a broad family of 12 benchmark instances with divergentto-general supply chain networks under four lead-time regimes show that PPO consistently delivers the best overall performance in terms of total cost, especially as the network becomes larger, more interconnected, and more uncertain. The results further indicate that reduced observation designs improve scalability in complex settings and that mixed action parameterizations can enhance solution quality with only moderate computational overhead. Overall, this study demonstrates that DRL is a promising and scalable methodology for coordinating inventory and routing decisions in real-world multi-echelon supply chains with flexible replenishment structures.

title: Hedging with Talent: How Selection Under Uncertainty Reshapes Automation's Workforce Effects
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) - College of Engineering and

detail.title: Hedging with Talent: How Selection Under Uncertainty Reshapes Automation's Workforce Effects
detail.abstract: When automation arrives at workplaces where workers can easily exit, job insecurity theory predicts they should flee. Across automation deployments at the fulfillment organization we studied, temporary workers did not. The candidate worker-side explanations for this puzzle---improved working conditions and reduced labor market alternatives---find no support in our evidence. We document an upstream organizational mechanism---that we call hedging with talent---comprising two coordinated practices: managers facing operational uncertainty at automation deployment concentrate their most reliably observed workers against the uncertainty reliability hedging, while shielding workers from the automation context that would let them self-select information shielding. Hedging with talent is a general response to automation in temp-labor settings; what novelty contributes is duration. Through a mixed-method study combining administrative data on 59,021 temp worker separations across 21 automation deployments with 351 interviews and 718 hours of observation, we trace the mechanism through hire-cohort decomposition across ten deployment sites. Across all sites, incumbents (workers hired before deployment who separated after) showed elevated tenure relative to fresh hires---the structural signature of selection from the observed pool. At the focal novel-technology site, the depth and duration of incumbent retention substantially exceeded the patterns at comparable mature-sortation sites: 22.4 percent of Gallifrey incumbents reached 2,000 hours of cumulative tenure against an upper bound of 9.0 percent at comparable mature-sortation sites; 13.5 percent of Gallifrey incumbents lasted more than a year past the deployment date, against an upper bound of 0.4 percent at sites with comparable observation windows. A second site with concurrent novel and mature deployments showed directionally consistent patterns. What appears to be worker behavior at automation deployments is, on inspection, management action working through an information system workers cannot see---a structural process that operates broadly across automation deployments and that novelty distinctively sustains.

detail.abstract:
European debates on competitiveness increasingly treat corporate law as a lever to help innovative firms scale. The European Commission’s Proposal for a new “28th regime” seeks to introduce an optional, EU-wide corporate legal form designed, inter alia, to facilitate the cross-border scaling of innovative firms. A central instrument of the Proposal is the use of model articles of association to be adopted through future implementing acts. This Article argues that, while standardised articles may ease incorporation and lower drafting costs for ordinary unlisted firms, they fall short for VC-backed companies—the very cases that motivated the initiative.

Building on prior work on venture capital contracting under mandatory corporate law, we identify four shortcomings. First, the architecture is incomplete: the Proposal omits a model shareholder agreement, even though effective VC contracting depends on the interaction between articles of association and shareholder arrangements. Second, the drafting process is overly generalist and unlikely to yield genuinely VC-specific templates. Third, the Proposal’s fairness-oriented logic risks producing terms that clash with the asymmetric, state-contingent structures typical of VC deals. Fourth, the legal protection offered by the template is limited, focusing on formation-stage effects while leaving subsequent judicial intervention unconstrained.

We propose four adjustments: introduce a model shareholders’ agreement; create a dedicated VC drafting track; abandon fairness as the organising principle for VC templates; and provide a robust safe harbour covering both ex ante design and ex post enforcement.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that modern corporations, particularly Big Tech Platform Corporations (BTPCs), should be understood not as private contractual arrangements but as artificial legal entities created and empowered by States. Through incorporation, corporations receive State-like attributes including perpetual existence, legal personhood, capital lock-in, and entity shielding, enabling them to accumulate and organise capital across time and space. The paper introduces the concepts of “Recursive Capital” and “Capital-Constituting Corporations” to explain how BTPCs extend beyond market participation to shape the very conditions under which economic activity becomes capitalisable. Drawing historical parallels with the English East India Company and Gilded Age monopolies, the paper contends that BTPCs now exercise infrastructural and governance power comparable to semi-sovereign actors. Existing antitrust and contractual theories are therefore inadequate. The paper concludes that platform governance requires structural regulation and a reassertion of democratic oversight to recalibrate the delegated powers States have granted corporations.

title: What California's Senate Bill 253 Means for Asset Managers
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business, Hankuk University of Foreign Studies and University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business

detail.title: What California's Senate Bill 253 Means for Asset Managers
detail.abstract: Asset managers serving climate-conscious investors rely on carbon-intensity metrics to guide capital allocation within sectors, but until now have compared firms primarily on Scopes 1 and 2 emissions—direct operations and purchased energy—because that data was most available under voluntary reporting. California's Senate Bill 253 changes that, mandating full-scope emissions disclosure, including Scope 3, for U.S.-incorporated firms with over $1 billion in annual revenue doing business in California. Our study in Nature Communications Sustainability shows that adding value-chain emissions fundamentally alters relative carbon performance evaluation, with partial and full sector-peer rankings correlating at just 42%. In sector-neutral carbon-tilted portfolios, full-intensity tilting cuts financed emissions by roughly 45% versus only 6% on partial-intensity data, at comparable returns. This synthesis evaluates what these findings mean for asset managers and the climate-conscious investors they serve, arguing that the choice of emissions metric shapes a portfolio's fundamental and carbon characteristics.

detail.title: Corporate National Identity

detail.abstract:
What makes a corporation American, Italian, Chinese, or any other nationality – and who gets to decide? In the contemporary global economy, corporate national identity (CNI) can no longer be understood as a fixed legal attribute. Rather, it emerges from the interaction of four interrelated facets – legal, economic, (geo)political, and symbolic – whose relative salience varies across contexts and over time. Classical legal tests such as the jurisdiction of incorporation, real seat doctrine, and corporate control remain important, but they are increasingly insufficient. In a world of weaponized interdependence, data location and access, supply-chain geography, state influence over private firms, and efforts to shape public perceptions of corporate identity now play central roles in determining how firms are classified and treated. Two nascent tests are emerging across these facets: what might be called a “data seat” doctrine that treats data location and access as a marker of CNI, and a government influence test that looks beyond voting equity to assess the degree of state leverage over corporate decision-making.

Drawing on case studies involving TikTok, Shein, Pirelli, and Nippon Steel’s acquisition of U.S. Steel, the article illustrates how CNI is increasingly contested and actively reconstructed. The result is a potential shift away from a binary world in which cross-border transactions are either permitted or blocked, toward a more intrusive model in which states restructure governance arrangements midstream in the name of national security, while firms seek to strategically shape their identities to navigate this new reality. The article explores new questions CNI contestation and engineering raise for corporate law, investor protection, and cross-border investment.

detail.title: Advancing Competition Policy in the Digital Gatekeeper Era – A Tribute to Heike Schweitzer
detail.abstract: This contribution examines Heike Schweitzer’s role as a competition policy analyst and adviser in the formative phase of European competition policy towards digital platforms. It situates her work in this context and develops a conceptual framework that captures the challenges of analysis under conditions of uncertainty and dynamic market developments. Through a selective analysis of four key reports, the article reconstructs central analytical approaches and policy proposals, identifies characteristic features of a “Heike Schweitzer approach”, and assesses its influence on subsequent regulatory developments, in particular the Digital Markets Act and section 19a of the German Competition Act.

title: Framing AI in public innovation: the engagement-manipulation nexus
affiliations: University of Edinburgh, Pan-Atlantic University and Epam Systems Colombia SAS

detail.title: Framing AI in public innovation: the engagement-manipulation nexus
detail.abstract: AI integration into public service innovation creates a paradox: promising enhanced engagement while risking manipulation. This paper develops the Engagement-Manipulation Nexus, a conceptual framework using Framing Theory to analyse this tension. We adapt Framing Theory to the algorithmic era, arguing AI is both an object to be framed and an agent disseminating frames. AI innovation trajectories are forged through communicative struggles among actors deploying competing frames. This paper contributes a novel theoretical framework, theorizes public innovation as communicatively constructed, and provides a diagnostic tool for practitioners. Critical frame awareness is essential for steering AI towards public value and democratic governance.

title: What Creates Safe and Efficient Pedestrian–Vehicle Interactions? A Naturalistic Study to Design Human-Like Behaviour for Automated Vehicles
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Leeds and University of Leeds

detail.title: What Creates Safe and Efficient Pedestrian–Vehicle Interactions? A Naturalistic Study to Design Human-Like Behaviour for Automated Vehicles
detail.abstract: Safe and efficient interaction with pedestrians is critical for the successful deployment of autonomous vehicles (AVs). While vehicle speed and acceleration are vital communication signals for this interaction, the ways in which human drivers use this kinematic communication signals remain under-explored. To design motion-based communication for AVs, this study aims to explore how drivers control their speed as a function of initial interaction conditions, and how this translates into more or less successful interaction outcomes. We analysed naturalistic trajectory data of vehicles and pedestrians from two zebra crossings in Leeds, UK, comprising 981 interactions. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was applied to quantify the mediating effect of vehicle kinematics on the relationship between initial time gap and interaction outcomes (crossing order, efficiency, and safety). Based on these models, vehicle speed profiles associated with optimal and worst outcomes were identified and compared using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE). PLS-SEM results confirmed that vehicle kinematics significantly mediate interaction outcomes, exerting a strong influence on efficiency and safety, and a weaker influence on crossing order. Minimum vehicle speed in particular exerted a strong influence on crossing order and safety, suggesting that the speed to which the driver drops is a key communication signal to pedestrians. The mediation results and trajectory analysis revealed that drivers used different strategies to achieve balance between their efficiency and interaction safety: in yielding scenarios (time gap > 3 s), they decelerated early and softly to maintain a low non-zero speed (~1 m/s) at a far distance (>10 m) to ensure safety while conserving momentum to ensure efficiency; in ambiguous non-yielding scenarios (time gaps ~ 1 – 3 s), they employed a two-stage strategy: a proactive initial deceleration to prepare for potential danger and reduce uncertainty, followed by an assertive acceleration for efficiency; in unambiguous non-yielding scenarios with a narrow time gap (< 1 s), they sacrificed a small amount of efficiency and adopted proactive deceleration before pedestrians displayed a clear crossing intention to ensure safety. This study expands the understanding of interaction beyond binary yielding choices, offering new insights into the proactive strategies human drivers use to negotiate right-of-way safely and efficiently. Emulating these kinematics strategies can support better integration of AVs into human traffic.

title: Price Discovery Leadership and Structural Fragility: Investment-Grade Credit Leads High Yield in the March 2020 Liquidity Crisis

detail.title: Price Discovery Leadership and Structural Fragility: Investment-Grade Credit Leads High Yield in the March 2020 Liquidity Crisis
detail.abstract: Applying the structural warming framework of Yun (2026b) to HYG (iShares iBoxx High Yield Corporate Bond ETF), we document a counter-intuitive lead-lag relationship in structural fragility: investment-grade credit (LQD) exhibits a spread volatility inflection 7 trading days before high yield credit (HYG) during the March 2020 liquidity crisis. LQD's structural warming signal begins February 24, 2020, with a 13-day lead over the March 9 limit-point bifurcation. HYG's signal begins February 28, with a 6-day lead. Both instruments snap on the same date. The finding is consistent with LQD's role as the price discovery venue for investment-grade credit (Yun, 2026a): the venue that carries the structural load of institutional hedging and flight-to-quality flow absorbs stress first. We also document a consistent 4x volatility ratio at the structural yield point across both instruments (LQD: 4.0x, HYG: 4.3x), suggesting a candidate universal threshold at which dealer intermediation fails regardless of credit quality. A methodological finding accompanies the empirical result: daily spread standard deviation is the correct structural signal for both instruments; daily maximum spread is contaminated by auction microstructure noise in HYG and unreliable as a fragility indicator.

title: The Paradox of Cooperative Migration Diplomacy in the Global South: Inter-Sending State Cooperation, Multilevel Diplomacy Strategies, and the Philippine State

detail.title: The Paradox of Cooperative Migration Diplomacy in the Global South: Inter-Sending State Cooperation, Multilevel Diplomacy Strategies, and the Philippine State
detail.abstract: How and why do sending states in the Global South cooperate under anarchy? Despite their significance, IR scholarship has largely overlooked the sending states' strategic logic and use of labor migration as a foreign policy tool. Using the Philippine state as a single case study, I argue that Global South sending states strategically manipulate complex interstate power dynamics to solidify inter-sending state coalitions and enhance bargaining power by employing multilevel cooperative diplomacy-bilateral (learning), multilateral (cooperation), and global (positioning). Methodologically, I employ semi-structured interviews (N = 15) with state and nonstate actors, process tracing, secondary sources, and decade-long field observations. Rather than viewing migration diplomacy as zero-sum, the Philippine state adopts a positive-sum, human-rights-centered migration diplomacy, fostering global coalition-building while pursuing material and ideational interests. title: Inequality, Business Cycles, and Growth: A Unified Theory of Fiscal Stabilization Policies

detail.title: Inequality, Business Cycles, and Growth: A Unified Theory of Fiscal Stabilization Policies
detail.abstract: Do tax-financed fiscal expansions entail a trade-off between short-run output stabilization and long-run growth? To answer this question, we develop a heterogeneous agent framework with nominal rigidities and endogenous growth. Analytically, we characterize three regimes with potentially opposing effects on output and technology growth, depending on systematic monetary policy and tax incidence. In the U.S., the quantitatively relevant regime features a robust tradeoff: a typical fiscal expansion, financed by higher tax progressivity, yields an impact output multiplier above one, a near-zero multiplier after three years, and sizable long-run output losses. Taxing the middle class avoids this trade-off and maximizes welfare.

title: Propagation Risk and Structural Sensitivity in Supply Chain Networks
affiliations: University of Florida - Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering and University of Florida - Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering

detail.title: Propagation Risk and Structural Sensitivity in Supply Chain Networks

declarations.funderStatement: The authors acknowledge support from NSF award No. 2534856.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how productivity shocks propagate through a Cobb-Douglas supply-chain network with inventories and intermediate inputs. In the unconstrained economy, the aggregate response to a sectoral productivity shock is characterized by the standard Hulten-Domar effect. We introduce a constrained propagation framework in which one sector's output is fixed at its baseline level. The resulting expression shows that the constrained aggregate response equals the unconstrained effect minus the component transmitted through the constrained sector. This leads to a shock-specific bottleneck measure that identifies sectors acting as transmission channels, rather than merely as shock origins. We also derive the sensitivity of aggregate output to variations in input-output link weights in the unconstrained economy. We then apply the framework to BEA input-output data and show that constrained bottleneck rankings differ from standard sector-importance rankings. Combining these rankings with shock probabilities estimated from Fama-French industry returns yields a forward-looking sector-protection rule. The results suggest that constrained propagation and link sensitivity provide a tractable framework for supply-chain risk management.

title: Globalization, Borders, and the Limits of RTAs in Africa

detail.title: Globalization, Borders, and the Limits of RTAs in Africa
detail.abstract: This paper examines the dynamic trade effects of RTAs in Africa within the broader context of globalization. Using a dynamic gravity model that accounts for international borders and geographic factors, the results indicate that RTAs led to a 670% increase in intra-African trade over 45 years. However, when border-related frictions capturing the effects of globalization are included, the trade impact drops to 260%, supporting the view that the large average trade effects of RTAs in Africa cannot be explained by tariff reductions alone. The analysis also uncovers significant trade diversion effects when non-tariff barriers are considered, challenging the conventional view of RTAs as net welfare-enhancing in Africa.

title: Measuring Institutional Closure in Public Procurement: A Network-Based Index from European Buyer-Supplier Data
affiliations: , Aristotle University of Thessaloniki - Faculty of Medicine, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki and Aristotle University of Thessaloniki - Department of Economics

detail.title: Measuring Institutional Closure in Public Procurement: A Network-Based Index from European Buyer-Supplier Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available administrative data and does not involve human participants. No ethical approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Public procurement systems generate detailed administrative records that capture how contracting authorities interact with suppliers over time. While most empirical work uses these data to study outcomes such as prices, participation, or efficiency, less attention has been paid to the structural patterns through which procurement systems sustain repeated buyer-supplier relationships across contracting cycles. We introduce the Institutional Closure Index (ICI), an authority-level structural indicator that identifies when procurement is both concentrated within a limited supplier base and stabilized through persistent, embedded authority-supplier ties. By integrating supplier concentration with relational persistence and embeddedness, the ICI captures configurations that standard concentration or participation metrics cannot detect in isolation. Applying the ICI to Tenders Electronic Daily (TED) award data for EU above-threshold procurement (2018-2022), we document strongly right-skewed and domain-specific patterns of closure. High-closure configurations are concentrated in particular procurement contexts and tend to arise as upper-tail phenomena within domains rather than as uniform system-wide regimes. These patterns emerge within formally open procurement frameworks, highlighting the distinction between procedural openness and the structural reproduction of supplier relationships. The ICI is designed as a descriptive monitoring tool rather than a performance score. It provides a comparative signal that can support governance and oversight by benchmarking authorities within procurement domains and identifying where stable and concentrated buyer-supplier configurations may warrant targeted, contextsensitive follow-up.

title: Immigration Generations and Perceptions of American Courts: Unpacking Complex Generational Effects

detail.title: Immigration Generations and Perceptions of American Courts: Unpacking Complex Generational Effects
detail.abstract: Immigrant perspectives on the criminal justice system have garnered significant scholarly interest in recent years. Yet, the trust levels of different generations of immigrants in American courts remain inadequately explored. Utilising data from the General Social Survey 2018, this study compares the levels of trust in American courts and confidence in the United States (U.S.) Supreme Court among first-, second-, and third-generation immigrants with those of the native-born group. The analysis considers several control variables, such as institutional confidence, general trust, attitudes towards penalties, and demographics. Findings reveal that firstgeneration immigrants exhibit greater trust in American courts than native-born individuals. Meanwhile, second-generation immigrants display lower confidence in the U.S. Supreme Court compared to their third-generation immigrant and native-born counterparts. All control variables influenced trust in American courts. Confidence in Congress and television, trust in people, age, and educational attainment impacted confidence in the U.S. Supreme Court. Finally, holding immigrant generations constant, Blacks expressed lower trust in American courts and less confidence in the U.S. Supreme Court than Whites, Hispanics, and Asians, and Asians demonstrated lower confidence in the U.S. Supreme Court relative to Whites and Hispanics.

title: Creative Destruction after the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami: Evidence from the Maldives
affiliations: University of Bologna - Department of Economics and University of Bologna - Department of Economics

detail.title: Creative Destruction after the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami: Evidence from the Maldives
detail.abstract: We study the long-run macroeconomic effects of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami in the Maldives (1995-2019). After an initial GDP contraction of about 9%, the economy not only recovered but steadily exceeded its pre-disaster path, indicating a sustainable recovery beyond pre-tsunami trends (+50% in 2011-2019). In the long run, the economy grows monotonically faster, consistent with a creative-destruction process (+5.2 p.p.). Tourism-sector evidence shows persistent increases in receipts per arrival without comparable growth in tourist volumes, suggesting quality upgrading rather than scale expansion. These findings support build-back-better reconstruction policies as drivers of sustained post-disaster development.

title: The Challenges of Blockchain Arbitration from a Private International Law Perspective
affiliations: Public University of Navarra (UPNA)

detail.title: The Challenges of Blockchain Arbitration from a Private International Law Perspective
detail.abstract: This paper aims to explore the emergence of Blockchain Arbitration and the legal challenges it poses from a private international law perspective. It examines the legal implications of this new type of arbitration, its feasibility under international regulatory frameworks (including the European Union, the United States and the 1958 New York Convention), and assesses leading decentralised justice platforms such as Kleros, Aragon and Jur. The study highlights the fundamental differences between blockchain arbitration and traditional arbitration, identifying challenges such as the absence of a seat, the anonymity of parties and arbitrators, and the tension between decentralisation and legal oversight. Finally, it explores future trends and proposes recommendations to adapt existing regulatory frameworks, concluding that while blockchain arbitration will not replace classical arbitration in the short term, it could establish itself as a valuable complement to resolve disputes in the global digital economy.

title: Financial Well-being and Inclusion of Justice Involved Populations: Evidence from the SHED

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2026-024, 2026[10.17016/FEDS.2026.024]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This study examines financial challenges faced by justice-involved individuals using 2023-2024 Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking data. Individuals with justice system contact experience substantially worse financial outcomes than those without criminal records, with disparities widening by severity of involvement. Compared to individuals with no prior records, those arrested but not convicted are 4 percentage points less likely to report doing at least okay financially, while formerly convicted as well as incarcerated adults are 15 percentage points less likely. Formerly incarcerated individuals are also 21 percentage points less likely to have credit scores above 660 and 13 percentage points less likely to have credit cards. These disparities mirror patterns observed across education levels, where adults with lower educational attainment experience lower financial well-being and inclusion. Our findings document substantial barriers to financial stability among justice-involved populations and may inform policies promoting financial inclusion and improving economic outcomes for this group.

title: Double Descent and Benign Overfitting in Macroeconomic Forecasting
affiliations: Queen Mary, University of London, University of Salzburg and Brandeis University - International Business School

detail.title: Double Descent and Benign Overfitting in Macroeconomic Forecasting
detail.abstract: We study double descent and benign overfitting in macroeconomic forecasting. We document that double-descent risk curves arise in standard macroeconomic datasets that are driven by a small number of latent factors, and we characterize when the underlying benign-overfitting mechanism holds. The conditions of Bartlett et al. (2020) are satisfied under the exact factor model and can also hold under the more realistic approximate factor model, provided idiosyncratic variances are not too dispersed across series. Because macroeconomic panels have only moderate dimensions, the overparameterization ratio N/T required by the theory is not naturally available. Our solution is to augment the data with synthetic copies from an estimated factor model and we prove that this strategy converges to a kernel ridge regression with a factorstructured kernel. Using monthly (FRED-MD) and quarterly (FRED-QD) US data, the resulting estimator consistently outperforms the Stock-Watson factor model for point forecasting across all series and horizons, with gains that are pervasive, statistically significant, and increasing with the forecast horizon. Our results suggest that benign overfitting, when it works, succeeds because overparameterization implicitly constructs a well-behaved kernel, not because overparameterization is intrinsically desirable.

title: The Effect of the Federal Reserve on the Stock Market: Magnitudes, Channels and Shocks

detail.abstract: We survey and extend work on the Federal Reserve’s effect on the stock market, focusing on three empirical findings: The effect of monetary policy surprises in a narrow window around announcements from the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the pre-FOMC announcement drift, and the FOMC cycle in stock returns. We discuss the magnitude of the Fed’s impact (directional effects or effects on average stock returns), the types of shocks coming from the Fed (pure monetary policy shocks, reaction function news, or information about the Fed’s view of the economy), and the asset pricing channels through which effects emerge (an equity premia for news from the Fed, or changes to yields, equity premia, or expected dividends). We also consider the information transmission (communication) channels. The Fed’s effect on the stock market is large, even for average stock returns earned over periods of several decades. Fed-induced changes to both yields and equity premia play substantial roles, with less direct evidence available regarding cash flows. For stocks, reaction function news appears to be more important than Fed information effects. Communication flows outside announcements windows are important.

detail.abstract: We consider the impact of state laws that prohibit conduct already barred under federal law. In particular, we examine the effectiveness of state minimum legal sales laws for tobacco, or tobacco 21 laws, implemented after the federal T21 law in December 2019. detail.abstract: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses (SRMAs) are important tools for evidence synthesis but have historically required substantial manual effort, particularly during the data extraction phase. To address this bottleneck, we developed and evaluated an automated pipeline that utilizes large language models (LLMs) to ingest full text scientific articles and extract structured metadata. We benchmarked the performance of leading models, including Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and Sonnet 4.0, across two distinct domains: mobile health interventions and education. Our results indicate that Gemini 2.5 Pro achieved the strongest performance in qualitative metadata extraction and outcome identification. However, quantitative metadata extraction remained a significant challenge. Models struggled to interpret complex data across multiple tables and failed to calculate effect sizes when only raw figures were reported. Crucially, we find that human annotators often applied implicit filtering criteria not documented in the coding manual, which made benchmarking the results challenging. We discuss the implications of these findings, emphasizing that while LLMs can accelerate the coding process, reliable automation requires significantly more prescriptive coding manuals to strictly steer model behavior and ensure fair benchmarking.

title: The Origins of American Counties. Part III: The Southern States

detail.title: The Origins of American Counties. Part III: The Southern States
detail.abstract:
Part III: This is the third of five papers of a book in progress, "The Origins of American Counties: A Fifty-State Tour of the History and Perseverance of America's Least Understood Local Governments." For a full introduction, see Part I, "Theory and New England." My book explains why counties were formed in a complex dance between localities that wanted to be a county seat and state legislatures eager to control their territory, and then frozen within rigid configurations in the twentieth century. My method is to examine in detail the historical origins of the two smallest counties-by land area and by modern population-in each state. These represent the main problems that modern observers see in counties: underpopulated rural counties and urban counties that do not encompass their metropolitan areas. 

The South consists of those states where slavery was legal up to the Civil War. Slavery and its plantation legacy engendered pervasive state control, largely administered by county governments, which discouraged other forms of local government. Post-Civil War reformers attempted to establish Northern-style townships, but they were discarded after Reconstruction, replaced in most cases by the unimportant "magisterial districts." Because the dominant political interests were rural plantation owners, obtaining the county seat was less important than establishing a county for state representation. Counties rather than cities command the loyalties of Southerners The northeast-to-southwest order in which the sixteen southern states are discussed is Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, Arkansas, and Missouri.

detail.title: Informality and Patronalism in Mexico: A Theoretical Sketch and Background Material for the Political Capitalisms Project
detail.abstract: This study applies the Magyar-Madlovics theoretical framework of patronal politics to the Mexican case, extending the analysis beyond its original post-communist scope to examine how informal patronal networks operate in Latin American contexts. While both post-communist and Latin American regions exhibit significant informal and patronal relations that shape political and economic outcomes, their historical starting points differ fundamentally. The post-communist region experienced the collapse of state socialism and subsequent privatization processes, while Latin America developed through colonial legacies, oligarchic capitalism, and negotiated transitions from authoritarianism. This study examines Mexico's federal and subnational political dynamics from approximately the 1970s to the present, analyzing how patronal networks function across different territorial levels and interact with formal political institutions.

title: I Don't Recall: Information and the Governance Tradeoffs in Securities Lending

detail.title: I Don't Recall: Information and the Governance Tradeoffs in Securities Lending
detail.abstract: Institutional investors are commonly viewed as facing a tradeoff between revenue and voting power when lending shares. However, lending also generates valuable voting information via the borrowing demand of informed short sellers.  I develop a model in which lenders trade off revenue, voting power, and information, and derive novel implications for corporate governance. Contrary to conventional wisdom, expected firm value can suffer when lenders recall shares to cast extra votes, since doing so discourages borrowing ex-ante and thereby reduces the informativeness of those votes; the key governance tradeoff is between a larger number of less informed votes and a smaller number of more informed votes. Thus, share lending and voting are not necessarily substitutes — they can also be complementary.

title: Informality and Patronalism in the Regimes of the Middle East: A Theoretical Sketch and Background Material for the Political Capitalisms Project

detail.title: Informality and Patronalism in the Regimes of the Middle East: A Theoretical Sketch and Background Material for the Political Capitalisms Project
detail.abstract:
This study extends the Magyar–Madlovics theory of patronal autocracy beyond its original post-communist scope by developing a typology of patronal autocracies based on distinct forms of political legitimation. Challenging the mainstream comparative paradigm, the analysis departs from three implicit axioms of liberal-democratic political science: the presumed separation of political, economic, and communal spheres; the coincidence of formal and informal power positions; and the assumption of the state as an actor oriented toward the public interest. By dissolving these axioms, the study conceptualizes patronal autocracy as a regime type organized around informal patron–client hierarchies that structure power across institutional boundaries.

Building on Max Weber’s classical typology of legitimacy, the paper argues that patronal autocracies cannot be adequately understood through a single legitimating logic. In addition to substantive rational legitimation—identified in post-communist contexts—the analysis introduces traditionally legitimated and charismatic-theocratic variants of patronal autocracy. On this basis, the study distinguishes three ideal-typical forms: (1) traditionally legitimated patronal autocracies, exemplified by the Gulf monarchies; (2) charismatic-theocratic patronal autocracy, represented by the Islamic Republic of Iran; and (3) substantive rational patronal autocracies, encompassing both post-communist “mafia states” and military-bureaucratic regimes.

The proposed typology strengthens the explanatory power of the patronal autocracy framework by demonstrating its universal applicability across regions with divergent historical, cultural, and institutional backgrounds. Rather than treating Middle Eastern and post-communist regimes as analytically exceptional, the study situates them within a unified conceptual space, showing how different legitimating foundations shape the institutional carriers, normative status, and operational logic of patronal rule.

detail.abstract: Local efficiency need not imply cross-sectional efficiency. I study economies where each firm is priced rationally under local information and public cross-sectional signals. Unless aggregation is perfect, dispersed learning about a common state leaves residual Bayesian filter errors. Expected excess returns are zero under local pricing filtrations, but proportional to this information aggregation wedge under the pooled cross-section. Because observable characteristics proxy for these errors, book-to-market, profitability, investment, and past returns predict returns without being risk premia or behavioral mistakes. This single wedge explains why anomalies have a strong factor structure, why firms migrate across value and growth portfolios, why value operates primarily within industries, why anomaly returns concentrate on news days, and why the Security Market Line appears flat. Characteristic arbitrage cannot make prices cross-sectionally efficient; only perfect aggregation can-but perfect aggregation destroys the dispersed learning that generates predictability.

detail.abstract: We study tariffs in a general equilibrium dynamic model with search frictions between heterogeneous exporting producers and importing retailers. We show the model has a unique equilibrium and analytically characterize home unilateral import tariffs that maximize welfare given a passive foreign country. Search frictions add two terms to the standard optimal tariff expression: One lowers tariffs when contact rates are low; another when private export costs exceed social opportunity costs. Search frictions also introduce new incentives to subsidize imports due to market thickness effects. We calibrate our baseline to U.S. and Chinese 2016 data. We compare this baseline to a counterfactual with international search costs reduced to domestic levels but with all other parameters fixed. We find that higher baseline search costs reduce optimal U.S. unilateral and Nash tariffs and attenuate welfare responses to tariff changes.

detail.abstract: Modern innovation increasingly emerges not within individual firms but across (digital) business ecosystems, where multiple independent actors co-produce knowledge and value whilst competing over the distribution of innovation rents. This article argues that existing legal frameworks to protect and promote innovation, particularly intellectual property (IP) law and competition law, were designed for a more linear, standalone model of innovation and are poorly suited to the relational, ecosystem-embedded and cumulative nature of contemporary innovative activity. Drawing on innovation economics, business ecosystem theory, competition and IP law, the article advances three interconnected arguments. First, in regimes of 'shared' and 'open' innovation, IP rights should give rise not solely to exclusionary entitlements but also, in appropriate circumstances, to compensation rights calibrated to reflect the contributions of all ecosystem participants. Second, competition law and IP rights should be reconceived as institutional complements rather than antagonists, each reinforcing the conditions for sustained cumulative innovation. Third, and most innovatively, the article proposes the tokenization of IP and data access rights - including data tokens, IP rights tokens, and innovation rent tokens built on blockchain infrastructure - as a concrete legal technology for operationalizing this framework. Tokenization enables fractional ownership of innovation rents, reduces transaction costs in fragmented IP landscapes, facilitates collateralization by ecosystem participants, and converts exclusionary property rules into compensatory liability rules, thereby aligning legal entitlements with the distributed, cumulative reality of shared innovation. The article calls for a differentiated legal architecture that combines exclusivity and compensation according to ecosystem structure, actor position, and innovation stage.

title: Personalized Dynamic Pricing with Demand Learning: The Impact of Growing Effective Dimensionality

detail.title: Personalized Dynamic Pricing with Demand Learning: The Impact of Growing Effective Dimensionality
detail.abstract: In this paper, we investigate personalized dynamic pricing and demand learning under high-dimensional models with growing effective dimensionality. Compared to strictly sparse models with a small and constant number of true predictors, allowing the number of effective features to grow can capture richer relationships through which an individual customer's demand can depend on the customer's features. Motivated by dynamic pricing applications where sellers typically have access to an expanding number of relevant customer features, we consider a seller that dynamically sets the price of a product for every individual customer. Customers arrive sequentially over time, and the seller observes a vector of features for each arriving customer. Demand is governed by a personalized model that depends on these customer features, and we measure the seller's performance by regret, defined as the revenue loss relative to a clairvoyant who knows the underlying personalized demand model. We establish theoretical regret bounds for this setting and complement them with numerical experiments that illustrate the role of growing effective dimensionality.

detail.abstract:
This study investigates how global institutional investors respond to gender diversity and climate risk concerns in Korean firms through disclosed voting rationales and how these disclosures subsequently influence corporate policies. We find mixed results.

First, voting rationale disclosures are more sensitive to gender diversity concerns than to climate risk. Specifically, investor opposition citing gender diversity decreases as the ratio of female directors rises. However, opposition citing climate risk does not increase in response to higher total CO2 emissions.

Second, we find that voting rationale disclosures have a limited influence on gender or climate-related corporate policies. While opposition citing gender diversity appears to prompt increases in the number and ratio of female directors in subsequent years, this pattern is confined to large firms subject to gender quota laws and is observed only during the years preceding the law's implementation. Furthermore, we find that opposition based on climate risk concerns is associated with subsequent reductions in total CO2 emissions, but only for small firms. Lastly, the publication of a sustainability report is associated with higher firm value when global institutional investors do not issue opposing rationales against management proposals, but this association holds only for small firms.

detail.abstract:
National security exceptions have long been part of international trade law, but their use has expanded alongside the rise of economic statecraft. States now increasingly rely on geoeconomic tools such as sanctions, subsidies, tariffs, and investment and export controls to pursue geopolitical goals. This phenomenon, described by political scientists as “weaponized interdependence,” has blurred the boundary between economic policy and national security, thereby straining the integrity of WTO rules and the multilateral trading system.

Against this backdrop, how can states promote rule-of-law values such as transparency and predictability on the international plane as they implement geoeconomic policies?

This Article makes two contributions to the international law literature. First, it advances global administrative law scholarship by underscoring the relevance of procedural principles in domains often treated as exceptional and by showing how recurring regulatory practices across legal systems can inform early-stage conversations around transnational economic security governance.

Second, the Article complements international economic law scholarship by identifying a set of procedural norms embedded in the domestic administration of trade and investment security: agency findings, notice and transparency, consultation, proportionality, temporal limits, periodic review, and neutral oversight. Drawing on a comparative analysis of seven jurisdictions—China, Japan, the Netherlands, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the European Union—the Article examines how these shared procedural features interact with existing multilateral frameworks and suggests that they provide a pragmatic basis for managing economic security measures in a deeply contested global order.

This study provides a systematic analysis of how the circular economy is framed in the climate-mitigation context of the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report using a mixed-methods approach that combines computational text analysis with qualitative content analysis through sentence-level manual coding. detail.abstract: This paper provides novel evidence on how income inequality shapes the heterogeneity of US monetary policy spillovers to GDP across foreign economies. Using state-dependent local projections and exploiting variation in disposable income inequality across a panel of 87 countries over the period 1966-2020, we show that household heterogeneity influences how foreign GDP responds to a US monetary policy tightening. GDP contracts by up to one and a half times more when inequality is above average. However, while higher inequality amplifies negative spillovers in advanced economies, it mitigates them in emerging markets. To rationalise this finding, we use a three-country open economy Two-Agent New Keynesian (TANK) model, which suggests that this divergence is driven by differences in participation in international financial markets. Households in emerging market economies face greater barriers to international investment, limiting their ability to re-balance portfolios towards higher-return foreign bonds after the shock.

detail.abstract: Despite concerns that many older adults delay essential financial decisions, there is limited population-level evidence linking measured procrastination to late-life behavior. Using the first nationwide procrastination module in the Health and Retirement Study, we show that individuals with higher procrastination scores are significantly less likely to engage in core estate-planning tasks. Procrastinators are about nine percentage points less likely to have a will or trust and report lower retirement satisfaction, controlling for demographics, income, and region. We validate the behavioral measure by showing that procrastinators report worse health and exhibit some riskier behaviors, consistent with theoretical predictions. Together, these results highlight procrastination as a meaningful behavioral constraint that shapes financial and health outcomes at older ages.

detail.title: Accurate Estimation of Small Effects: Illustration Through Air Pollution and Health
detail.abstract: This paper identifies design parameters that can lead to inaccurate estimates of small effects. Low statistical power not only makes such effects difficult to detect but resulting significant estimates necessarily exaggerate true effect sizes on average. Through the literature on short-term health effects of air pollution, I explore this issue and its policy implications. Exaggeration can be substantial and power low even with large sample sizes. Real-data simulations highlight key additional drivers: the number of exogenous shocks, instrument strength, and outcome count. I propose a workflow to evaluate and mitigate exaggeration risk in non-experimental studies.

title: Housing Prices, Monetary Policy and Banking Crises: Nonlinear Dynamics, State Dependence and Policy Trade-offs

detail.title: Housing Prices, Monetary Policy and Banking Crises: Nonlinear Dynamics, State Dependence and Policy Trade-offs
detail.abstract: This study examines the joint effects of housing market dynamics and monetary policy on systemic banking crises using annual panel data for 26 advanced and emerging economies over 1990-2023. Applying fixed effects binary logit, multinomial logit and local projection methods, we find consistent evidence of non-linear relationship between growth rate of housing price and crisis probability. Moderate price appreciations are stabilizing while excessive growth becomes destabilizing beyond indicative range of 17-22 percent, which declines to 8-14 percent under contractionary monetary conditions. Monetary tightening is consistently associated with higher crisis risk. Notably, housing prices act as contemporaneous amplifiers rather than early warning indicators having stronger effects during crisis periods. The findings highlight state dependent risks and underscore the need for coordinated monetary and macroprudential policies to mitigate housing driven financial vulnerabilities.

title: Transition Pain or Structural Decline? Causal Evidence on Renewable Energy and Employment in U.S. Legacy Regions

detail.title: Transition Pain or Structural Decline? Causal Evidence on Renewable Energy and Employment in U.S. Legacy Regions
detail.abstract: The green penalty hypothesis holds that expanding renewable energy capacity destroys employment in legacy fossil fuel and manufacturing regions by raising compliance costs and accelerating industrial decline. We provide a methodologically rigorous test of this hypothesis at the U.S. state level, applying a Double Machine Learning (DML) architecture to a balanced annual panel of all fifty states over 1997-2023. A Random Forest algorithm partials out a highdimensional vector of macroeconomic, demographic, and political confounders in the first stage, while two-way demeaning eliminates unobserved state fixed effects and common time shocks prior to estimation. Identification is robust to repeated cross-fitting across one hundred random partitions. We find no statistically or economically significant effect of renewable energy penetration on state unemployment rates in either Rust Belt manufacturing states or coaldependent extraction states. This null result survives substitution of alternative first-stage estimators, restriction to the pre-pandemic period, lagged treatment specifications of up to two years, block cross-validation, and systematic jackknife sensitivity analysis of the cluster definitions. A mechanism test further rules out that the presence of a large extractive sector conditions the transition-employment relationship. Comparing Random Forest and Ridge Regression first stages, we show that inflated green penalty estimates in prior work are attributable, at least in part, to functional form misspecification in the nuisance function rather than genuine causal effects. The structural unemployment observed in legacy regions is consistent with market forces (routine-biased technological change, secular manufacturing decline, and broader energy market disruptions) that are independent of renewable energy policy. Effective intervention requires active labour market policies calibrated to the occupational and geographic distance between declining fossil fuel roles and growing sectors, embedded within a well-resourced Just Transition framework.

detail.abstract: India's National Pension System (NPS) converts part of accumulated defined-contribution wealth into annuity income, making decumulation design a question of both predictability and adequacy. This paper studies one product-specific case: a nominal joint-life annuity without return of purchase price, with 60 per cent spouse continuation, for an age-60 annuitant and age-57 spouse, over May 2013 to March 2025. Using contemporaneous 10-year Government of India yields and the common Indian Individual Annuitant's Mortality (IIAM) 2012-15 schedule, the paper converts the constructed payout series into a purchase-time money's-worth ratio (MWR) and measures realised Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) purchasing-power retention after purchase. The joint-life payout ranges from 7.19 to 8.30 per cent; the MWR ranges from 0.783 to 1.031 and averages 0.890. Mean real retention is 0.95 after one year, 0.86 after three years, 0.78 after five years, and 0.61 after ten years. Quoted payout rates, actuarial value, and realised real-income retention therefore measure distinct aspects of decumulation. A supplementary 10-year exercise reports residual liquidportfolio burden under fixed spending assumptions. The contribution is a product-specific measurement framework for NPS decumulation design, not a welfare ranking or full market evaluation.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of Agentic AI on operational performance in commercial banks across the United States and the United Kingdom between 2022 and 2026. It investigates whether autonomous systems function as net value creators or as amplifiers of systemic risk. Using a systematic review of secondary sources, including industry reports, regulatory publications, and institutional disclosures, the study identifies a consistent but underexplored pattern: performance outcomes vary significantly by task type. To explain this variation, the paper proposes the Ambiguity Threshold Hypothesis (ATH), which suggests that Agentic AI delivers reliable gains in low-ambiguity, rule-based tasks, while producing unstable or adverse outcomes in high-ambiguity, judgment-intensive environments. The paper further introduces a temporal dimension to performance evaluation, arguing that reported benefits are typically front-loaded, whereas associated risks emerge over longer time horizons, leading to a systematic distortion in perceived net value. While the findings are based on secondary data and should be interpreted as directional rather than conclusive, the study highlights the limitations of current industry reporting and suggests the need for task-level evaluation frameworks in both the deployment and regulation of Agentic AI systems.

detail.title: Implications of Policy Interventions on Eliminating Gender Gaps *
detail.abstract: This paper studies policy interventions intended to eliminate gender differences in labor market outcomes, principally wages, through an equilibrium model of statistical discrimination with dynamic choices of education and labor market participation. The estimated model succeeds in matching observed gender gaps in wages, college attainment rates, the college premium and labor market participation rates. We quantify both the intended and unintended consequences of the policies through simulated interventions based upon the estimated model. In the short run the policy that requires gender free applications in the market for skilled labor eliminates wage gaps but once education choices respond the effects are attenuated. A more comprehensive policy that enforces gender free compensation reverses the wage gap in skilled markets and eliminates it in unskilled labor markets, even once education adjusts. These interventions impact college rates, the college premium gap and participation rates as well. The final section studies these interventions using a difference-indifferences (DID) approach to analyze the simulated data. With education fixed, the DID method recovers the policy effects but this is not the case once education adjusts, reflecting the effects of the intervention on both treated and control groups.

detail.abstract: We develop a model of index-linked rebalancing around reconstitution events. Index trackers trade off execution costs against tracking-error concerns, while speculators maximize profits given expected index-linked demand. The model shows speculators effectively act as liquidity providers at index reconstitution, and trading costs decline as speculator competition increases. With enough competition, even loose index trackers optimally rebalance at index reconstitution. The model rationalizes concentrated reconstitution-day trading with little contemporaneous price impact: speculators' pre-positioning shifts price pressure away from the reconstitution date. We estimate that avoidable rebalancing costs borne by index-linked investors are small relative to more general price impact estimates from the literature. We argue that apparent front-running reflects competitive liquidity provision and benefits index investors.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes Oman’s water sector through a microeconomic examination of Nama Water Services as a regulated natural monopoly. The study evaluates market structure, supply and demand conditions, pricing efficiency, and resource allocation using secondary data from the Nama Water Services Annual Report 2024 and other institutional sources. The findings indicate that water demand in Oman continues to increase due to population growth and economic expansion, while supply remains relatively inelastic because of infrastructure constraints and dependence on desalination. Despite improvements in operational performance, non-revenue water losses remained relatively high at 37.1% in 2024, reflecting productive inefficiency. In addition, treated wastewater reuse remained below potential levels, indicating inefficient resource allocation. The study also confirms that water demand is highly price inelastic, limiting the effectiveness of pricing policies alone in reducing consumption. The study concludes that improving operational efficiency, reducing water losses, expanding wastewater reuse, and supporting sustainable infrastructure investment are essential for strengthening long-term water security in Oman.

title: The Wisdom of the Few: Skilled Traders and Prediction Market Accuracy
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Wisdom of the Few: Skilled Traders and Prediction Market Accuracy
detail.abstract: We study how participant composition affects pricing accuracy in prediction markets using transaction-level data from Polymarket. We classify participants by execution behavior across markets. Makers post liquidity and bear adverse selection costs. Takers cross the spread. Switchers do both. A model where signal-holders choose their execution role rationalizes cross-market role-mixing as a behavioral signature of private information. Most switchers are indistinguishable from takers. A small subset, identified by a skill screen, drives the result. A one-standard-deviation increase in their volume share is associated with 19% lower pricing error at close. A Brier decomposition attributes the effect to price calibration, not to how well markets distinguish outcomes. These skilled switchers carry permanent price impact and earn improving returns with experience. Takers persist despite losses. Market accuracy traces to a thin layer of informed participants.
